f: not having the skill to write clearly or neatly
not having any sense of guilt or regret for sins
not having enough light to see by at dusk
r: Medieval Latin pēnūriōsus; see penury, from Latin penuria “want”
s: The poor penurious horde, naught in the cooking pot and naught in the belly.

f: a raised wooden stage; actors and musicians stand on it to perform at fairs
a paved courtyard behind a house; tables and chairs are arranged for dining outdoors
a shallow dish of earthenware; meats and vegetables are baked in it slowly
r: French parterre “on the ground”, from par “on” + terre “ground”
s: The window opened towards a most lovely garden, whose smooth turf and gorgeous parterres swept down to the river.

f: someone who travels on foot
someone who sells goods door to door
someone who trims horses’ hooves
r: Greek paidagōgós, from paîs “child” + agōgós “guide”
s: Jones chid the pedagogue for his interruption, and then the stranger proceeded.

f: relating to the work of miners or quarrymen
very small and finely detailed
done in a slow and graceful dance step
r: Late Latin minātōrius; compare menace
s: Number 3, Lauriston Gardens wore an ill-omened and minatory look.

f: a kiss of greeting
a spiced lamb stew
a woven prayer rug
r: Ottoman Turkish kısmet “fate, destiny”, from Arabic qisma “division, lot”
s: Sexualised Catholicism, at the dawn of MTV, was Madonna’s first stroke of kismet.

f: given to eating far more than is needed
having the smooth sheen of polished glass
covered with small lumps or swellings
r: Latin glūtinōsus; gluten + -ous
s: Then comes the dinner, a glutinous spread that seems simultaneously generous and disgusting, but no one ever touches the food.

f: suitable in size and shape
strong and in good health
filled with quiet contentment
r: fit “convulsion, seizure; sudden burst of activity” + -ful
s: Troubled by her unfinished work, she fell into a fitful sleep.

f: strong and full of tendons
hollow and filled with air
guilty and full of wrongdoing
r: Latin sinuōsus
s: We were entranced by her sinuous dance.

f: a long crusty loaf of white bread
a small leather case for carrying papers
a heavy wooden club for driving stakes
r: French bagatelle, from Italian bagattella
s: A young pianist sat down in a shuttered room in the capital of defeated Germany and played a Bagatelle by Beethoven.

f: a small round drum beaten with the fingers; carried by a minstrel at a feast or by a page in a procession
a low stool with three legs and a padded seat; used by a squire to help a knight mount his horse
a narrow strip of parchment bearing a short motto; hung from a lance or pinned to a knight’s helmet
r: Old French tabart “simple sleeveless overtunic”, of unknown origin
s: A knight on a black horse appeared, clothed in jet-black velvet, and with a tabard of black linen about him.

f: cooked in wine
served with mustard
baked with cream
r: French lyonnaise “in the manner of Lyon”
s: For dinner, we had beef with potatoes lyonnaise.

f: a lover who writes poems in secret to his beloved
a spice merchant who trades in incense and oils
a hermit who lives alone in a desert cave
r: Greek Murmidónes, via Latin Myrmidones
s: He cared no more for the Devil and all his myrmidons, for he kenned brawly he was damned.

f: grow weak and decay
cut off a limb
fill in a hole
r: Latin imputō “to bring into the reckoning, charge”
s: People impute great cleverness to cats.

f: painted in watercolor
thin and transparent
gaunt and haggard
r: French gauche “left, awkward”, from gauchir “to veer, turn”
s: Seeking by vulgar pomp and gauche display In 'good society', to make her way.

f: a large stone tomb with a pointed roof that was built for a king or a queen
a long rowing boat with a raised prow that carried pilgrims across the river
a tall clay jar with two handles that held oil or wine for long voyages
r: Greek Pháros
s: The house was not very felicitously titled, said many: it was no academic pharos.

f: fragrant and without any trace of sweat; freshly perfumed
complete and without any fault or flaw; carefully finished
fond of and attentive to formal rules; very punctual
r: Late Latin perfunctōrius “careless, negligent”, from perfungor “perform, carry through”
s: He did a perfunctory job cleaning his dad's car, finishing quickly but leaving a few spots still dirty.

f: gear for horses
readiness for war
a fine perfume
r: equi- + poise
s: To my mind, the textual arguments in this case are close to equipoise.

f: (of hatchlings) covered in down and able to leave the nest at once
(of seabirds) nesting on high cliffs and rocky ledges above the sea
(of songbirds) singing several notes at once in a high pitch
r: New Latin Altrices, from altrīx “nourisher”, from alere “to nourish”
s: First, humans are altricial, with immature newborns and a long childhood.

f: a brief speech given at the end of a formal banquet
a final payment made at the end of a business contract
a quiet walk taken at the end of a long day
r: post- + Latin lūdus “play”, modeled on prelude
s: In the Sibelian world of song, then, postludes would inevitably sound redundant or extraneous.

f: lacking a voice; especially unable to speak
lacking interest; especially showing no emotion
lacking hair; especially without feathers
r: a- “not; without” + photic
s: We need to classify bacteria as photic and aphotic.

f: a formal written record of a person’s family tree and ancestry
a formal written prediction of the end of the world
a formal written collection of short sayings or maxims
r: Greek apología “speech in defense of a position”; a doublet of apology

f: wrap a corpse in a burial cloth
wither and wrinkle with age
cry out in a high voice
r: Old English sċrīfan “to decree; (of a priest) to prescribe penance”, from Latin scrībō
s: If he have the condition of a saint and the complexion of a devil, I had rather he should shrive me than wive me.

f: a hired circus clown
a clumsy dance partner
a cheap cigar
r: US since the 1920s; popularized by Jack Conway of Variety
s: I ain't your friend, palooka.

f: the branch of theology that studies the lives and miracles of the saints and martyrs honored by the church
the branch of philosophy that studies the origin of the universe and the order of the heavens
the branch of theology that interprets prophecies about the end of the world and the last judgment
r: French théodicée, from Greek theós “god” + díkē “justice”; coined by Leibniz in 1710
s: The theodicy, the master-narrative, had become secularized.

f: so full of rage as to lose all self-control
so covered in rust as to be beyond repair
so rich in iron as to taste of metal
r: Middle English irkesome: irk + -some
s: He has this irksome habit of racing up to red lights, so he has to brake heavily.

f: rise above all others; surpass
speed up gradually; gain pace
plant seeds in rows
r: Latin accēdō “approach, accede”, from ad + cēdō “move, yield”
s: Maintenon had been governess to the children in the late 1670s before acceding to the king's favours.

f: darken; used mostly of evening skies
harden; used mostly of soil in frost
hasten; used mostly of riders
r: Old English hercnian, from *heorcian “to hark”
s: Dear mother Ida, hearken ere I die.

f: at no time
in no place
with no doubt
r: Middle English nowyse: no “none” + wise “way, manner”
s: This time at sea will nowise be lost.

f: a soft woollen fabric dyed bright red; used in hunting coats and to trim hats
a heavy leather apron worn by blacksmiths; used to protect against sparks and burns
a thick cream made from goat’s milk; used in baking and to enrich sauces
r: Old French boquerant “fine cloth”, probably ultimately from Bokhara in Uzbekistan
s: Four rogues in buckram let drive at me—

f: a spore that is freely carried by the wind in spreading mold to new places
a guest who is freely invited to dine at the table of a host
a task that is freely given to the youngest member of a household or crew
r: Medieval Latin fungibilis, from Latin fungor “to perform, discharge a duty”
s: The archetypical fungible is money.

f: a workplace where cloth is dyed by soaking and boiling
a workplace where grain is ground by turning millstones
a workplace where leather is cured by tanning and drying
r: Old Norse smiðja
s: Traditionally a village smithy was a busy place because the smith's work was so necessary.

f: a worker on a farm
a teller of stories
a writer of comedies
r: Old French cueriste, from cuer “choir”: choir + -ster
s: None of the new choristers can sing in tune but they will learn soon enough.

f: a country house; usually stands among vineyards on a hillside
a tent camp; usually set up beside a river for soldiers
a covered market; usually stands in the main square of a town
r: Italian campanile “bell tower”, from campana “bell”
s: The Leaning Tower of Pisa is a campanile.

f: relating to gardens
shaped like an hourglass
harshly scolding
r: Middle French hortatoire, from Latin hortor “encourage”
s: Not in a curse but in a hortatory appeal.
